Meta-Analysis Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/meta-analysis.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(metafor)
library(dplyr)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

apa_parameters and apa_performance make APA-style tables of meta-analyses fit with metafor::rma:

Table Function Contents
Studies and pooled estimate apa_parameters Each study’s effect size, confidence interval, and weight, followed by the pooled estimate
Meta-regression apa_parameters Coefficients of the moderators, as for other regression models
Heterogeneity apa_performance k, Q, τ2, I2, and, for meta-regressions, the test of the moderators and R2
Subgroups apa_subgroups Each subgroup’s pooled estimate and the test of subgroup differences
Publication bias apa_publication_bias Egger’s regression test, the rank correlation test, and trim and fill, with adjusted estimates

Studies and the Pooled Estimate

The dat.molloy2014 data set in the metadat package (installed with metafor) has the correlations between conscientiousness and medication adherence in 16 studies. Correlations are meta-analyzed as Fisher’s z values (measure = "ZCOR" in escalc), and slab gives the study labels:

d_adherence <- escalc(
  measure = "ZCOR",
  ri = ri,
  ni = ni,
  data = metadat::dat.molloy2014,
  slab = paste(authors, year)
)

fit_adherence <- rma(yi, vi, data = d_adherence)

apa_parameters(fit_adherence) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Each study’s correlation and confidence interval, and the pooled estimate below the rule, are converted back from Fisher’s z to r. The weights are each study’s percentage of the total weight in the random-effects model. The note names the measure and the model, and it gives the test of the pooled estimate, its 95% prediction interval (the range in which the true effect of a new study is expected to fall), and the test of heterogeneity.

The column of effect sizes is named by the measure given to escalc: for example, g for standardized mean differences ("SMD"), r for correlations ("COR" or "ZCOR"), and OR, RR, or IRR for odds ratios, risk ratios, and incidence rate ratios. Ratios are analyzed on the log scale and exponentiated for the table. With transform = FALSE, estimates stay on the scale on which they were analyzed (e.g., log risk ratios). With weights = FALSE, the weights are left out.

Heterogeneity

apa_performance gives the heterogeneity statistics:

apa_performance(fit_adherence) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

With metrics = "all", the table adds τ, H2, and confidence intervals of τ2 and I2.

Ratio Measures

In the dat.landenberger2005 data set (Landenberger & Lipsey, 2005), 58 studies compared the number of juvenile and adult offenders who reoffended after a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) program and after no program. The effect sizes are odds ratios (the odds of reoffending after CBT divided by the odds without it), which are analyzed on the log scale and exponentiated for the table:

d_recidivism <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = n.cbt.rec, bi = n.cbt.non, ci = n.ctrl.rec, di = n.ctrl.non,
  data = metadat::dat.landenberger2005,
  slab = study
) |>
  mutate(
    Sessions = sessions,
    Program = factor(program,
                     levels = c("demo", "practice", "research"),
                     labels = c("Demonstration", "Practice", "Research"))
  )

fit_recidivism <- rma(yi, vi, data = d_recidivism)

apa_parameters(fit_recidivism) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Odds ratios below 1 mean that fewer offenders reoffended after CBT. Across the studies, CBT reduced the odds of reoffending by about a third.

Meta-Regression

Moderators are added with mods. Programs differed in how often they met, so here the number of CBT sessions per week is a moderator:

fit_sessions <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ Sessions, data = d_recidivism)

apa_parameters(fit_sessions) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
apa_performance(fit_sessions) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

For a meta-regression, apa_parameters shows the intercept and moderators, as for other regression models. Coefficients (B) are on the scale on which the effect sizes were analyzed (here, log odds ratios), and for ratio measures, the exponentiated coefficients are added (here, OR): each additional session per week multiplies the odds ratio by about 0.93, so programs that met more often reduced reoffending more. apa_performance adds the omnibus test of the moderators (QM) and the percentage of heterogeneity they explain (R2), and QE is the test of the heterogeneity that remains.

Subgroup Analysis

A subgroup analysis compares the pooled estimates of groups of studies. The CBT programs had been set up for demonstration, for research, or as routine practice. apa_subgroups pools each group of studies and compares them:

apa_subgroups(fit_recidivism, Program) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Programs set up for demonstration or research reduced reoffending more than programs in routine practice.

By default, each subgroup has its own τ2, and the subgroups are compared with Qbetween, the heterogeneity of the subgroup estimates. With tau2 = "common", the subgroups share one τ2, which is estimated more precisely when subgroups have few studies: the estimates come from a meta-regression with the subgroup as a categorical moderator, and the subgroups are compared with its omnibus test (QM). The subgroup variable can be a column of the data (quoted or unquoted) or a vector (e.g., d_recidivism$Sessions > 1).

Publication Bias

apa_publication_bias tests for publication bias (small-study effects) and gives estimates adjusted for it, as computed by metafor: Egger’s regression test, with its limit estimate (the predicted effect of a study with a standard error of zero); Begg and Mazumdar’s rank correlation test; and trim and fill, with the number of studies it imputed (k0) and the pooled estimate with them included:

apa_publication_bias(fit_adherence) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

The adjusted estimates are on the same scale as the table of studies (here, correlations), and the note gives the unadjusted pooled estimate for comparison. Add "fsn" to methods for the fail-safe N, which is widely criticized and is not shown by default. These methods are available for rma models without moderators.

Multilevel Meta-Analysis

When studies report several effect sizes, the effect sizes are not independent, and a multilevel (three-level) model with rma.mv has a random intercept for each level. In the dat.konstantopoulos2011 data set, 56 schools in 11 school districts compared the achievement of students on modified and traditional school calendars (standardized mean differences). The table of a multilevel model has a row for each effect size, so this example shows only the pooled estimate (studies = FALSE):

fit_schools <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  random = ~ 1 | district / school,
  data = metadat::dat.konstantopoulos2011
)

apa_parameters(fit_schools, studies = FALSE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
apa_performance(fit_schools) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

apa_performance gives the variance of the true effects at each level (σ2, with the level as a subscript) and the multilevel I2(Cheung, 2014), the percentage of the total variability due to heterogeneity at all levels. With metrics = "all", the table adds σ and confidence intervals of σ2 for each level, and I2 for each level. Meta-regressions of multilevel models work as for rma. Random effects with an ~ inner | outer structure (e.g., correlated outcomes within studies) are not yet supported.

Citations in Notes

Some notes cite the articles that describe a method (e.g., trim and fill and the multilevel I2). In the console and in this article, the citations are written as text. To have them formatted and added to the reference list of a Quarto or R Markdown document, see Citations in notes in the regression article.

Options

  • method = "EE" in rma fits an equal-effects model; the table labels the pooled estimate accordingly, and there is no prediction interval or τ2.
  • test = "knha" in rma uses the Knapp–Hartung adjustment; the pooled estimate is tested with t, and the note says so.
  • studies = FALSE shows only the pooled estimate, with its test, instead of the study rows.
  • Multilevel models with random intercepts (rma.mv with random = ~ 1 | study / effect) are supported; random effects with an ~ inner | outer structure are not yet supported.

References

Begg, C. B., & Mazumdar, M. (1994). Operating characteristics of a rank correlation test for publication bias. Biometrics, 50(4), 1088–1101. https://doi.org/10.2307/2533446
Borenstein, M., Hedges, L. V., Higgins, J. P. T., & Rothstein, H. R. (2009). Introduction to meta-analysis. Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470743386
Cheung, M. W.-L. (2014). Modeling dependent effect sizes with three-level meta-analyses: A structural equation modeling approach. Psychological Methods, 19(2), 211–229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032968
Duval, S., & Tweedie, R. (2000). Trim and fill: A simple funnel‐plot–based method of testing and adjusting for publication bias in meta‐analysis. Biometrics, 56(2), 455–463. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2000.00455.x
Egger, M., Davey Smith, G., Schneider, M., & Minder, C. (1997). Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test. BMJ, 315(7109), 629–634. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.315.7109.629
